name: Padanjalinathar Temple, Tirukkanattumullur
deity: Shiva as Padanjalinathar (Patanjaleeswarar), with the goddess Kolavalaikkai Ambikai (Kanarkuzhali)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Chola Nadu on the northern bank of the Kollidam, sung in the Tevaram (8th century); structural temple with medieval and later additions
summary: Padanjalinathar Temple at Kanattampuliyur is the Tirukkanattumullur of Sundarar's Tevaram hymn, the quiet riverside shrine where the sage Patanjali is remembered as having been granted a second vision of Shiva's cosmic dance.

sections.history: Kanattampuliyur lies in the Kattumannarkoil country of Cuddalore district, on the northern side of the Kollidam, the great branch of the Kaveri. In the Tevaram the shrine is called Tirukkanattumullur, and it is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams on the strength of a decad sung here by the saint Sundarar, preserved in the Seventh Tirumurai. Its other great association is with the sage Patanjali, whose name the presiding Lord carries. The settlement's name is read in tradition alongside the puliyur shrines of the sage Vyaghrapada, though local sources tie this temple chiefly to Patanjali. The builders of the present stone temple are not firmly recorded; it has been raised and kept in worship by Tamil patrons across the medieval centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram, and outside the gateway lies the sacred tank known as Surya Pushkarini. Within, the sanctum of Padanjalinathar holds the Shiva linga, and the goddess is honoured as Kolavalaikkai Ambikai, also called Kanarkuzhali. The sacred tree of the shrine is the erukku. Temple accounts describe a Nataraja here whose pose is distinct, the left leg advanced and the body inclined slightly back, a form associated with Patanjali's vision. Facing the main sanctum stand an image of Patanjali himself and the four saints of the Tevaram, the Nalvar, so that the sage's devotion is kept before every visitor.
sections.legends: The legend of Kanattampuliyur belongs to Patanjali, the sage said to be Adisesha, the divine serpent, born as a human. He had been granted the sight of Shiva's cosmic dance at Chidambaram, but the longing it left in him did not rest. Tradition holds that he came on to this place and begged the Lord to show the dance again. Moved by his devotion, Shiva appeared here and danced for the sage alone, and the Lord has since been worshipped as Padanjalinathar, the Lord of Patanjali. Devotees remember the shrine as a place where a prayer, once answered, may be asked for a second time, and where steady longing is itself a form of worship.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri in February or March is kept with night-long worship, and Tirukarthikai in November or December fills the shrine with lamps. The Annabhishekam of the month of Aipasi, in October and November, anoints the linga with offerings of cooked rice. Tiruvadhirai in December or January honours Nataraja, the form of the Lord so closely tied to this temple's story. Monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Kanattampuliyur is a small, quiet village shrine, and the visit is an unhurried one. Enter beneath the eastern gopuram, pause by the Surya Pushkarini outside, and come to the sanctum of Padanjalinathar before turning to the goddess. Look for the image of Patanjali facing the sanctum, and for the Nataraja whose unusual stance is the heart of the temple's story. Devotees of dance, yoga and the inner life of the Shaiva tradition often come here for the sage's sake. The countryside around is green and the temple keeps the stillness of a place far from the main roads.

visit.timings: Typically open for a few hours in the morning and again in the early evening, with a long midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is near Muttam village in Kattumannarkoil taluk, Cuddalore district, about 9 km from Kattumannarkoil. Buses from Chidambaram and Kattumannarkoil reach Muttam, from where the temple is a short distance away; a local auto or taxi is advisable. Chidambaram is the most convenient railhead, and the nearest airports, at Puducherry, Tiruchirappalli and Chennai, are some hours away by road.
